title: The Civic Bestiary
description: A field guide to the characters of the body politic: portmanteaus for performative patriotism, bad-faith debate, hypocrisy, and algorithmic radicalization - plus the documented fallacies they commit.
preface: This is a bestiary, not a dictionary. The characters in it are real, common, and close by - the flag hoodie in the school-board queue, the centrist with one newsletter, the commentator monetizing your uncle's anger. Each species is named the way a naturalist would name it: by the trait that makes it unmistakable, and by the psy-loop it runs.

Two rules keep the guide from collapsing into a list of insults. The species is a pattern, not a person - a costume that wears people, not a kind of human, and one you can catch yourself in. And every entry describes a mechanism you could point at in a transcript, a rally, or a comment thread, so the name stays a tool for recognition rather than a way to end an argument.

The coinages are portmanteaus on purpose: legible on first contact, slightly ridiculous on second thought. Some of these characters are trolls in the old sense, things that live under bridges and demand a toll; some are trolls in the newer one. Both are field-observed here. That is roughly the right posture for the subject.

The fallacies work the other way round. They are not coinages and are not ours: they are documented errors in reasoning, named by logicians and studied by psychologists, and every one of them links to its source. Each chapter ends with the documented errors its own characters commit, so the joke arrives with its receipt attached. The definitions here are written in this guide's voice, but nothing in them is invented - if a claim about a fallacy cannot be traced to the literature, it does not go in the record. The errors that turn up in several chapters at once get a chapter of their own, because an error that belongs to everyone is one nobody flinches at any more: that is chapter V, and it is the chapter about the room rather than the people in it. The coinages are the joke; the fallacies are the part you can cite.

chapters.title: Performative Identity & Weaponized Liberty
chapters.note: The first chapter is about costume. Its species perform a loyalty they do not hold, or claim a liberty they will not extend: the flag on the truck, the pin on the lapel, the word that proves which side you are on. The tells are verbal and sartorial, because a performance is built to be read from a distance by somebody who will never check it. The moves turn an argument into a loyalty test, and the abilities are the machinery that makes the test binding. Read it as a wardrobe, not a roll call.

chapters.title: Bad-Faith Debate & Epistemic Breakdown
chapters.note: The largest chapter, and the one the guide is named for. Its species argue without intending to be convinced: the sophistroll who knows the fallacy is a fallacy, the illogician who does not, the decorumancer who polices the tone instead of the claim, the gallopologist who answers volume with volume. Every tell here is something you could transcribe, which is the only way to tell a bad argument from a person having a bad day. The fallacies behind the seam are the ones these species commit most, and the moves are the ways an argument gets ended without being answered.

chapters.title: Hypocrisy, Revisionism & Authoritarian Submission
chapters.note: This chapter is about the record: who keeps it, who edits it, and who is believed when the two disagree. Its species revise what they said, apologise without conceding, and submit to an authority they claim to despise. The tells are documentary - the deleted post, the corrected transcript, the non-apology that names the reaction instead of the act - because a revisionist needs an archive to revise. The abilities are the ones that make the record expensive to obtain: the NDA, the qualified immunity, the SLAPP, and the judge who was chosen for the case.

chapters.title: Fearmongering, Grift & Algorithmic Radicalization
chapters.note: The chapter about attention, and who is selling it. Its species manufacture fear and then convert it: the demagogue who needs the threat, the martyr who needs the wound, the plutocrat-martyr who needs both, and the algorithm that will feed all of them to whoever stays. The habitats are the rooms where the conversion happens, from the feed to the panel to the spin room, and the abilities are the policy that keeps the supply coming: the forever war, the manufactured doubt, the lobby, the oil deal. Read this one as an economy rather than a mood.

chapters.title: Normalization, Numbness & the Noise Floor
chapters.note: Every other chapter points at a character and the errors they commit. This one points at the room: the species who keep it exactly as it is, and the machinery that does the keeping - the soft launch that makes a change official, the clause that exempts what came before, the conference where the consensus is catered, the fatigue that ends the argument by exhausting it. Its fallacies are the ones that turn up in several chapters at once, because an error everyone commits is one nobody flinches at any more. Normalization is what a body politic does with the unacceptable once the flinching stops.

chapters.title: The Keystones
chapters.note: Every character in chapters I to IV has a counterpart with a job title: the clerk who keeps the record, the auditor who reads the books, the poll worker who counts in public. This chapter is the other side of the ledger. Its keystones are the offices whose presence holds an ecosystem together and whose absence is the whole problem; its remedies are the procedures those offices run, written down so they can be repeated by someone who is tired. Read this chapter when you want to know what to defend, and what to do on a Tuesday afternoon.
